questions.q: A search box filters all n product names with startsWith on every keystroke. The customer has typed L characters. What does one keystroke cost?
questions.explain: Every name is checked, and each check compares up to L characters. Built-in methods still do that work. A trie makes finding the prefix O(L), independent of n.
options: O(L)
O(log n)
O(n × L) in the worst case, and never less than one comparison per product
O(1), because startsWith is built in

questions.q: In a trie, what does the path from the root to a node represent?
questions.explain: Each edge is one character, so a path spells a string. Every word that starts with that string passes through the same node.
options: The number of words stored
A prefix: the characters on the edges, in order
The alphabetical rank of a word
A hash of the word

questions.q: Why does each trie node need an end flag?
questions.explain: "car" ends at a node that also has children (for "card", "care"). Without a flag you could not tell a stored word from a mere prefix, and has("ca") would wrongly say yes.
options: To know when to stop the whole trie
Because a word can be a prefix of another word ("car" and "card"), so reaching a node does not mean a word ends there
To mark leaves, since every word ends at a leaf
To store the word's length

questions.q: A trie holds 5 million product names. What does checking whether a 12-character name is present cost?
questions.explain: Lookup follows one edge per character, each an O(1) average Map lookup. The number of stored words never enters the cost.
options: O(log 5,000,000), about 22 steps
About 12 steps: one edge per character, whatever the number of names

questions.q: How many nodes (including the root) does this trie have?
questions.explain: root, t, e, a (tea), n (ten), o (to): 6 nodes. "tea" and "ten" share "te", all three share "t", and inserting "tea" twice creates nothing new.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The "car" path exists (it leads to card and care) but no word ends there, so it is a prefix and not a word. "cart" breaks off at the missing "t".
options: false true true false
true true true false
false true true true
false false true false

questions.q: How can a trie answer "how many products start with sam?" in O(L) instead of walking the whole subtree?
questions.explain: Insert increments the count on every node of its path; delete decrements it. Then the count at the prefix node is the answer, found by walking only the prefix.
options: By storing the words in a sorted array as well
By keeping in every node a count of the words that pass through it, updated on insert and delete
By hashing the prefix
It cannot; counting always needs the subtree

questions.q: Each node counts the words passing through it. What does this print?
questions.explain: All four words start with "s", two with "so", one with "sa". The empty prefix is the root, whose count is the number of words.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's insert first check whether the word already exists?
questions.explain: Creating nodes is idempotent (existing ones are reused), but incrementing counts is not. Checking first keeps the counts equal to the number of distinct words.
options: To make insert faster
Otherwise inserting the same word twice would increase every count on its path twice, and prefix counts and size would be wrong from then on
Because Maps cannot hold duplicate keys
To keep the words sorted

questions.q: Why is withPrefix written as a generator, and suggest stops after limit results?
questions.explain: After one typed letter, thousands of products may match. A generator produces results one at a time, so the caller can stop after five, and the walk never touches the others.
options: Generators are faster than arrays
The search box shows only a few suggestions; stopping early avoids walking the rest of a possibly huge subtree
Generators sort the results automatically
Because recursion is not allowed in classes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A generator runs only when the next value is requested. After break it is never resumed, so only two products were ever produced. That is how suggest avoids walking the rest of the subtree.

questions.q: Children are visited in alphabetical order of their character. In what order do these names come out?
questions.explain: Character by character, "10" starts with "1", which sorts before "2". A trie walked alphabetically gives the same order as a plain string sort. Numeric order needs a different comparison (localeCompare with { numeric: true }) or ranking.
questions.code:
const names = ["Tecno Phone 2", "Tecno Phone 10", "Tecno Phone 1", "Tecno Phone 20"];
console.log([...names].sort().join(" | "));
options: Tecno Phone 1 | Tecno Phone 10 | Tecno Phone 2 | Tecno Phone 20
Tecno Phone 1 | Tecno Phone 2 | Tecno Phone 10 | Tecno Phone 20
Tecno Phone 2 | Tecno Phone 10 | Tecno Phone 1 | Tecno Phone 20
Tecno Phone 20 | Tecno Phone 10 | Tecno Phone 2 | Tecno Phone 1

questions.q: You want the three best-selling products for any prefix, and short prefixes are typed constantly. Which design answers fastest?
questions.explain: Precomputed lists make a suggestion O(L): walk the prefix, read the list. The cost moves to memory (k entries per node) and to updates, which is a good trade when reads vastly outnumber writes.
options: Walk the whole subtree and sort all matches by sales
Store in every node the top three products of its subtree, updated when data changes
Keep the products in a Map by name
Sort the whole catalogue by sales once, and filter it by prefix on each keystroke

questions.q: A buggy delete decrements the counts along the path before checking that the word exists. What happens when you delete a word that is not in the trie?
questions.explain: Deleting "cart" when only "card" exists would decrement "c", "a" and "r" before discovering there is no "t". Check that the word exists (its end node has end set) before changing anything.
options: Nothing; the loop stops at the first missing character
Counts on the part of the path that exists are decreased although no word was removed, so prefix counts become wrong
The trie throws an error
The root is deleted

questions.q: The trie holds "car" and "card". You delete "car". What should change?
questions.explain: "card" still needs every node of "car". Only the fact that a word ends at r goes away. Removing nodes would delete "card" too.
options: Remove the nodes c, a, r
Remove only the r node
Remove no nodes: clear the end flag on the r node and decrement the counts on the path
Nothing, because "car" is a prefix of "card"

questions.q: This delete prunes a node as soon as its count reaches 0. What does it print?
questions.explain: Nodes c, a, r, d, t were created (5, plus the root makes 6 in total). Deleting "card" prunes d (6 − 1 = 5). Deleting "cat" prunes t, leaving root, c, a, r: 4. The "car" nodes stay because "car" is still a word.

questions.q: What goes wrong if delete clears the end flag but never removes unused nodes?
questions.explain: Unused nodes are harmless for has, but a catalogue with constant churn would keep every node ever created. Counts make pruning easy: a node with count 0 is used by no word.
options: Lookups return wrong answers
Lookups stay correct, but memory grows forever as products come and go: a memory leak
The trie becomes unbalanced
Nothing at all

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both display as "Café", but one uses "e" plus a combining accent (two code points) and the other a single "é". A trie compares code points, so without normalising both to the same form (NFC) the search misses.
options: false true 5 4
true true 4 4
false false 5 4
false true 4 4

questions.q: Keys are lower-cased and NFC-normalised on insert. What must happen to the customer's query?
questions.explain: A trie only matches identical characters. Whatever folding you apply to keys (case, Unicode form, accents, spaces), apply the same function to the query. The lesson's class does this by calling Trie.key in every method.
options: Nothing; the trie handles it
The exact same normalisation, or queries with capitals or the other Unicode form will not match
It must be upper-cased
It must be split into words

questions.q: How many trie edges would each loop create for this product name?
questions.explain: The emoji is one code point but two UTF-16 units, so indexing sees 6 "characters" and would split the emoji into two meaningless halves. for...of iterates by code point, giving 5.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: NFD splits each accented letter into a base letter plus a combining mark; \p{Mark} removes the marks; then lower-casing. Use the folded form as the key and keep the original name as the value to display.
questions.code:
const fold = (text) => text.normalize("NFD").replace(/\p{Mark}/gu, "").toLowerCase();
console.log(fold("Crème Brûlée"), fold("CAFÉ") === fold("cafe"));
options: creme brulee true
crème brûlée true
creme brulee false
Creme Brulee true

questions.q: A trie of 24,000 product names has 26,062 nodes for 400,880 characters. Why can it still use more memory than the plain array of names?
questions.explain: Node count is not memory. Per-node overhead dominates, so a trie is compact only relative to its number of nodes. Long keys with little sharing make it much worse.
options: Because tries store every word twice
Each node is an object with a Map (easily 100+ bytes), while a string stores a character in one or two bytes
Because the counts are stored as BigInts
It cannot; fewer nodes always means less memory

questions.q: What does a radix tree (compressed trie) change?
questions.explain: "samsung " as eight single-child nodes becomes one edge. It saves the most for long keys with little branching, such as URL paths, which is why web routers use radix trees.
options: It stores words in reverse
It merges chains of single-child nodes into one edge labelled with a whole string
It uses a hash of each word instead of characters
It keeps nodes sorted by popularity

questions.q: What is the compact alternative to a trie for "first k names with this prefix"?
questions.explain: All names with a prefix sit next to each other in sorted order. A lower-bound binary search finds the first in O(L log n), and the next k are the answer. It uses far less memory than a trie, but inserting costs O(n).
options: A Set of names
A sorted array: binary search for the first name ≥ the prefix, then read forward while names start with it
A linked list
A max-heap of names
A hash map from each prefix to its names

questions.q: Why can't a Map or Set of product names answer "names starting with sam" efficiently?
questions.explain: A hash map is excellent for exact lookups but knows nothing about prefixes or order. Tries and sorted arrays keep strings with a common prefix together.
options: Maps cannot store strings longer than 255 characters
Hashing scatters similar strings, so there is no place where all names with a prefix sit together; you must scan every key
Maps only support numeric keys
It can, with map.get("sam*")

questions.q: A customer types "smasung". What does a plain trie of product names suggest?
questions.explain: Tries match exact prefixes. Typo tolerance needs fuzzy matching (edit distance), which search engines add on top; a trie is the fast first layer, not the whole search.
options: Samsung products, because the letters are the same
Nothing useful: only the prefix "s" matches, and "sm" leads nowhere
An error
Every product

questions.q: Postcode zones "1", "10" and "100" have different rates. For postcode "105500", which zone applies, and how does the trie find it?
questions.explain: "100" does not match (the third digit is 5). Walking 1 → 0 → 5 passes rated nodes "1" and "10", and the path breaks at 5. The last rate seen belongs to the longest matching prefix. One pass, O(L).
options: "100", the zone with the most digits
"10": walk the postcode's digits, remember the last node that had a rate, and stop when the path ends
"1", the first zone found
None, because no zone is exactly "105500"

questions.q: Your autocomplete API is called on every keystroke by every visitor. Which production measure matters most?
questions.explain: High-frequency endpoints need bounded work per call: a result limit, a maximum prefix length and a rate limit. The trie should be built once (or in the background) and read many times.
options: Returning every match so the client can choose
Limiting the number of results and the query length, normalising the query, and rate-limiting the endpoint
Rebuilding the trie on each request so it is always fresh
Storing each request in the trie

questions.q: A trie of 2 million products is rebuilt from the database every night. How should the service switch to the new one?
questions.explain: Building off to the side means requests always see a complete trie, old or new, never a half-filled one. The old trie is garbage-collected once nothing refers to it.
options: Clear the live trie and insert the new products into it while requests keep arriving
Build the new trie separately, then replace the reference to the old one in a single assignment
Stop the service until the rebuild finishes
Merge the two tries node by node

questions.q: The lesson's random test uses words of 1 to 4 letters from the alphabet "abc". Why such a tiny alphabet?
questions.explain: With a large alphabet, random words rarely share prefixes and the tricky paths (delete "car" while "card" exists) are almost never exercised. Small alphabets make collisions the common case.
options: To make the test run in the browser
So that many words share prefixes and many are prefixes of other words, the cases where insert and delete bugs hide
Because tries only work with three letters
To avoid Unicode problems

questions.q: Finish insert(word) and has(word) for a trie of nodes { children: Map, end: boolean }. It should print true false true false.
questions.explain: Insert creates missing children along the path and marks the last node. has follows the path and returns the end flag: "tec" exists as a path but is not a word, and "tecno camon" breaks off after "tecno ".

questions.q: Finish insert (keeping a count on each node) and countPrefix. Inserting the same word twice must not change the counts. It should print 3 2 0 3.
questions.explain: Check for an existing word first, then increment the count of every node on the path, the root included. countPrefix is then one walk down the prefix: O(L).

questions.q: Finish suggest(prefix, limit): walk to the prefix node, then collect words below it in alphabetical order (visit children sorted by character), stopping as soon as you have limit words. It should print oraimo freepods | oraimo powerbank and then an empty line for "x".
questions.explain: Carry the text built so far with each node on the stack. Pushing children in reverse alphabetical order makes them come off the stack in alphabetical order. The loop stops at limit, so "oraimo smartwatch" is never visited. An unknown prefix returns an empty list, which prints as an empty line.

questions.q: Finish remove(word): return false and change nothing if the word is not stored; otherwise decrement counts along the path, prune the first node whose count reaches 0, or clear the end flag, and return true. It should print false true true | car,care | 5.
questions.explain: "ca" is only a prefix and "cat" is missing, so both are refused before any count changes. Deleting "card" prunes the d node; root, c, a, r and e remain: 5 nodes.

questions.q: Finish rateFor(postcode): walk the trie of zone prefixes along the postcode and return the rate of the longest matching prefix, or undefined. It should print 1500 2000 3000 undefined.
questions.explain: Remember the last rate passed and stop when the path breaks. Returning only when the whole postcode matches would find nothing; returning the first rate would always give the shortest prefix.

questions.q: Customers type in any case. Finish add(name) and lookup(query) so keys are lower-cased and NFC-normalised, but lookup returns the product's original name. It should print Samsung Galaxy A15 | Café Latte Mug | undefined.
questions.explain: The same key function is applied on the way in and on the way out, so different capitals and the decomposed "é" still reach the same node. The stored name doubles as the end marker: "samsung" is only a prefix, so its node has no name.
questions.expected: Samsung Galaxy A15 | Café Latte Mug | undefined

questions.q: Finish commonPrefix(words): insert all words into a trie, then walk down from the root while the current node has exactly one child and is not the end of a word. It should print ORD-2024-0 and then (none).
questions.explain: The common prefix is the chain from the root that never branches. Stopping at an end node matters too: the common prefix of "car" and "card" is "car", not "card". Building the trie is O(total characters).

questions.q: How many nodes does the trie have, and how many would a radix tree keep (the root, nodes where a word ends, and nodes that branch)?
questions.explain: root, p, h, o, n, e, s, t, o, s: 10 nodes. A radix tree keeps the root, the "o" after "pho" (it branches to n and t), and the four word ends. The chains "ph" and single steps like "n", "t" become labels on edges: "pho" → "ne" → "s" and "pho" → "to" → "s".

questions.q: Every node keeps the top 2 products of its subtree by sales. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every insert offers the product to every node on its path, and each node keeps its best two. "t" sees all four and keeps tablet (80) and tripod (65). "ta" and "to" each only ever saw one product. A suggestion is now just a walk down the prefix: O(L).
options: tablet,tripod | tablet | toaster | -
tv,tablet | tablet | toaster | -
tablet,tripod | tablet,tv | toaster | -
tablet,tripod,tv | tablet | toaster |

questions.q: Both searches find the products starting with "son". What does this print?
questions.explain: The naive filter compares 3 characters for each "sony" name, 2 for "samsung" and "sharp" (they fail at the second letter), and 1 for the others: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 12. The trie takes 3 steps to reach the "son" node, which has one child ("y"), however many products exist.

questions.q: The analytics team wants to know how many distinct prefixes customers' search terms have (every prefix of every term, not counting the empty one). That is exactly the number of nodes in a trie of the terms, minus the root. Finish distinctPrefixes(terms). It should print 7.
questions.explain: Each node below the root is one distinct prefix. "tv" and "tablet" share "t": t, tv, ta, tab, tabl, table, tablet = 7; "tab" and the second "tv" add nothing. A Set of all prefixes would give the same answer but store every prefix as a separate string.
